narrative:
The model determined that you have a 76.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest reasons pushing the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year, well below the average performance of students who were accepted. These low academic standings in law school sent the largest signals that you would struggle to pass the bar.

Your LSAT score was the third most influential factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 29.5, your score is noticeably below the 37.2 average of accepted students; however, this actually pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. Even so, it was not enough to overcome the much stronger negative impact of your class rankings.

In short, the model concluded that your academic performance during law school provided the clearest evidence of future difficulty with the bar exam.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Retake practice exams, seek academic support for bar preparation, and consider reapplying once you have demonstrable improvement in your study outcomes or a stronger practice-test record. Many students successfully improve their trajectory with targeted effort.
